prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with B003 first and B015 third, but after reading all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the top of my configuration. It is the one candidate where the original idea, the original experiment and the people are all identifiable and where I can be 'absolutely sure' of the record: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group then brought the instrument to the 10^-18 level and used it for many-body and gravitational-redshift measurements. It is an instrument that makes previously invisible effects measurable, with independent confirmation at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL and others, agreeing clock comparisons, and a pending redefinition of the second. All eight members ranked it, five in their top three, and nobody has raised a serious attribution objection. That breadth of support is not itself merit, but here it coincides with the cleanest experimental and attribution case on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology can look incremental next to a new phase of matter or a new astronomical window, and that the clock sits beside two earlier prizes (Hall and Hansch, frequency combs, 2005; Wineland, ion control and ion clocks, 2012). Contributors such as Lemonde, Derevianko and Takamoto, and ion-clock groups, could be argued to have claims, and the SI second has not yet been redefined, so a cautious member could wait. I think these are answered by the fact that the lattice-clock concept and its record accuracy are distinct achievements, but the committee should check this carefully. My own first choice, topological insulators (B003), has an equally strong physical case but a much less certain list of credited people.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because they are the most precise instruments ever built, the idea is distinct from the 2005 comb prize, and many groups have confirmed it with Sr, Yb and Hg.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and have moved toward it. I would add one qualification to the independent-confirmation argument: the replication is of the instrument performance, and the original experiment is Katori's, so the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice invention and not merely 'precision' in general. I also share your caution that Ye's contribution to stability, cavity stabilisation and many-body clocks is a separate step, and the citation should show both without inflating either.

responses.point: Pearce narrows B003 to Kane and Molenkamp, leaving out Xue to keep the credit focused, and puts IceCube first and optical clocks second.
responses.response: I respect the attribution discipline of cutting to two names, and it is a real improvement on the three-name list I opened with, because Xue's quantum anomalous Hall measurement is an independent experimental milestone rather than part of the original spin Hall observation. But a two-name topological prize leaves out Mele and Bernevig/Hughes/Zhang, which means the original-proposal record is still contested. That is why I now place B003 as an alternative and not first. On IceCube I disagree about ranking it above the clocks: the flux discovery is solid, but the credit for a kilometre-scale collaboration is much harder to pin to two people.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first as a discovery given by nature, while acknowledging that the credit among IceCube leaders, AMANDA, Baikal, ANTARES and DUMAND is not settled.
responses.response: I share the view that neutrino astronomy is a genuine new window, and I kept B014 as an alternative. My difficulty is exactly the one you state about internal credit. The prize is for those who did the original work, and for IceCube I cannot be sure that Halzen and Karle alone are the right people, nor that the source picture (one blazar, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) is mature enough. I would be happy to revisit it if the committee can document the decisive contributions of individuals.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as foundational physics and an enabling platform, with theory and experiment tightly linked in 2004.
responses.response: I do not dismiss it: strong coupling in a circuit was a new regime and the experiment is original. My reservation is the one you list yourself. Girvin and Huang are missing from the three-person cap, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits already honoured part of the same platform, so I would not rush a second superconducting-circuit award. I would be more persuaded if the committee could show that the transmon and dispersive readout, not just the strong-coupling demonstration, are covered by the credited trio.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first for their exact, universal character, while admitting that Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan and others make a clean three-person split contestable.
responses.response: The conceptual elegance is clear to me and the single-molecule pulling experiments do verify the relations. But those experiments came after the theorems, and by your own account the three-person split is contestable and Gallavotti and Cohen have a real competing claim. For a prize that must find 'the people doing the original work', I cannot rank it above candidates with a clearer record. Nobody else ranked it, so I would want a fuller attribution analysis before it could be a serious contender.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the credit of Lemonde, Derevianko and others requires a different citation wording.

Whether the topological insulator credit (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Xue, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) can be resolved into three or fewer names without a serious injustice, since B003 and B018 split the same field.
Whether the SI second redefinition timing should affect when lattice clocks are recognised.
Whether IceCube credit can be reduced fairly to Halzen and Karle.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the lattice clock candidate. I note that I work in electron microscopy at Chalmers and have no recorded collaboration with Katori or Ye; I have a general connection to the condensed-matter and materials community relevant to B003, B030 and B018, and Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is on the committee, but none of the credited names has a documented personal link to me.
